risk_of_bias.note: The primary evidence (one hair-analysis study of people who died of overdose; two studies of people on methadone) cannot be appraised from the reviews, and the claim about breaks rests on one study that the review itself reads as suggestive.

inconsistency.note: No conflicting statement in either review.

indirectness.note: Second-hand through narrative reviews, one of which cites the other; the settings named (incarceration, detoxification) come from the later review and are not in the review it cites.

imprecision.note: No estimate is claimed; the claim states that none is available.

rate.reasoning: A claim seen only through reviews starts from the design of the primary studies they describe, here observational (a hair-analysis comparison of people who died of overdose with people who were still using) and human studies of methadone, so it starts low, and is downgraded for risk of bias (primary studies not appraisable) and for indirectness (second-hand; one review cites the other). Certainty very low. The relation is insufficient evidence because neither source gives a size, a time course or a risk figure. Because every supporting anchor is a narrative review, the claim stays at draft and says so in its statement (METHODS 6.3). Status: single study in effect (Hickman et al. rest on White and Irvine for this point). The claim keeps to what the text says: White and Irvine name only a period of abstinence, and the examples of incarceration and detoxification belong to Hickman et al.
rate.population: People who use opioids (heroin, methadone and other opioids), as described in two narrative reviews; no primary study of a break from opioids was read
rate.exposure: A period without opioids (a period of abstinence in the reviews' wording) before use starts again
rate.comparator: Continued regular use; the same person's tolerance before the break
rate.outcome: Tolerance to opioid effects, including breathing depression, and the chance of a fatal overdose when use starts again
rate.magnitude: No estimate in either source. White and Irvine (1999), second-hand: one hair-analysis study (Tagliaro et al., 1998) found lower morphine content in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using (no numbers given in the review); the rate of loss of tolerance for euphoric, analgesic and respiratory effects is called sparse, probably uneven and possibly quick (receptor changes can occur in minutes or hours); incomplete tolerance to the breathing-depressing effect of methadone in two studies of people on methadone maintenance (Marks and Goldring, 1973; Santiago et al., 1977; no numbers given). Hickman et al. (2008): risk appears to be raised after periods of relative abstinence; no figures.
rate.short: Tolerance may drop during a break from opioids, two reviews say. So the usual amount may hit much harder, breathing included.
rate.rate: It's second-hand: two reviews, one citing the other, describe a few older studies that weren't checked here. Neither gives any numbers.

risk_of_bias.note: The trial (card sc_greenway_2024), RoB 2 some concerns: open label by necessity; sequence generation and allocation concealment not described; one usual-care patient excluded from analysis without a stated reason; more infusions missing without music (8 against 3), handled by inverse-probability weighting; who measured blood pressure, and whether they knew the group, not described. The review's studies were not appraised by the review and cannot be appraised here, and its highlights state benefits that its limitations disclaim (card sc_kheirkhah_2024).

inconsistency.note: Directions vary between the review's procedural trials (one null, one with more dreams or emergence reactions), as the statement says; the trial measured a different outcome.

indirectness.note: For the question asked (how a session feels, or how well treatment works), the trial reports only blood pressure, and its comparison was no music without a sound or attention control; the review's evidence is second-hand (METHODS §6.3) and mostly from ketamine given with other sedatives during procedures, often in children, and the only controlled ketamine-alone study used mothers' voices, partly spoken.

imprecision.note: One trial of 32 patients (interval for the smaller systolic rise 2.9 to 12.0 mm Hg); for how sessions feel, only small studies, mostly without a comparison group.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the trial was registered (NCT04701866), but its registry record and protocol supplement were not read, so the reported outcome was not compared with the registered one.

rate.reasoning: The best evidence is now one randomized trial, which starts high, but it answers only blood pressure: on its own, the smaller systolic rise with music would rate low (high, minus one for risk of bias and one for imprecision). For how a session feels, the evidence is still the review's small, mostly procedural studies seen second-hand (low, minus risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low). Rated for the claim as worded: down one each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, giving very low. Status single study: one randomized trial for blood pressure, and, for ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparison of listening with not listening (46 children under anaesthesia hearing recordings of their mothers' voices), seen through one review. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3), and every anchor has been checked by a second reader. The trial's secondary outcomes, deferred to later publications, have not been seen.
rate.population: 32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression receiving a clinical course of intravenous ketamine in Montreal (one randomized trial), and patients given ketamine or esketamine in clinical settings (anaesthesia, sedation, depression and alcohol-use-disorder treatment) in 14 earlier studies gathered by a scoping review
rate.exposure: Curated music throughout each 40-minute ketamine infusion (trial); music (or, in one study, recordings of mothers' voices) before, during or after ketamine or esketamine (review)
rate.comparator: Usual care without music (trial); no music (headphones with no recording, or a blank soundtrack) in most procedural trials and in the one comparison of ketamine alone; no comparison in the case reports and interview studies (review)
rate.outcome: Rise in systolic and diastolic blood pressure from the start to the end of each infusion (trial); anxiety, pain, emergence reactions, sedative use, dissociation and how the session was experienced (review)
rate.magnitude: Greenway et al. (2024), randomized, 181 infusions in 32 patients (31 apparently analysed for the primary outcome, editors' inference from the flow diagram): change in systolic blood pressure from 0 to 40 minutes, music against no music, β −7.4 mm Hg (95% CI −12.0 to −2.9), P = .008; diastolic β −0.8 mm Hg (printed 95% CI −1.59 to 3.18, an interval centred on +0.8, so its signs appear transposed), P = .58; read approximately from the figure, mean systolic rise about 11.5 mm Hg with music and 18.5 mm Hg without; no clinical, experience or depression outcome reported. Kheirkhah et al. (2024): no pooled estimates. 14 studies: 9 with other sedatives (music with less sedation and lower anxiety or pain in most; no effect on emergence reactions in one; more dreams or emergence reactions in another); 5 with ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparing listeners with children who heard nothing (46 children: mothers' voices against headphones with no recording), the rest case reports (3 patients) and interview studies (17 and 12 people). No study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression up to December 2023.
rate.short: Nobody knows yet whether it changes how a session feels or how well ketamine works. One trial found the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less with music.
rate.rate: One trial of 32 patients, reporting only blood pressure. The earlier studies are small, mostly during medical procedures, and known only through a review.

risk_of_bias.note: The site differences come from four overdose deaths chosen to illustrate the problem, with no denominator and no serial sampling (card sc_pounder_1990, JBI high); the ratios come from a compilation drawn mostly from published reports, some of them focused on poisonings, without study-level appraisal or uncertainty estimates (its number-weighted descriptive summaries do not supply study-level precision weighting or within-drug spread) (card sc_ketola_2019, AMSTAR 2 by analogy, critically low); the changes over time are relayed without sizes from a review that does not appraise its studies (card sc_borra_2026). Selection of striking cases could make the differences look larger than in ordinary deaths.

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: every source points the same way (levels differ by site and change after death); the size varies by drug, which the claim states rather than hides.

indirectness.note: The question concerns deaths involving any drug, including drugs used outside medicine; the compilation excludes cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids, the case series concerns large overdoses of medicines with drug still in the gut, and part of the evidence on timing is from animals.

imprecision.note: Four cases; no ranges, percentiles or intervals for any compiled ratio; many drug–specimen ratios rest on one to three results.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for case series and compilations of case literature.

rate.reasoning: A descriptive claim starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, which reaches the floor: very low. Strict reading: that drug levels can differ between sampling sites and change after death is shown consistently by independent designs (a case series with a sample from life, a large compilation of paired values, repeated-sampling studies as reviewed) and on its own would be rated low; the sizes, and how often a change matters in an ordinary death, are very low. Status replicated: Pounder & Jones and the primary studies compiled by Ketola & Kriikku and reviewed by Borra et al. are independent and agree in direction. Counted once: Pounder & Jones is one of the compilation's doxepin sources; Ferner (2008) takes its heart-to-femoral ratios from Leikin & Watson (2003), so the narrative reviews' ratios are one source, used only as second-hand examples.
rate.population: Bodies examined after death: four selected suspected overdose deaths at medico-legal autopsy (Pounder & Jones, 1990); 5,375 post-mortem cases from published reports and a Finnish laboratory database, 2000 to 2018 (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019); animal experiments and human bodies sampled more than once, as reviewed (Borra et al., 2026); narrative reviews (Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ferner, 2008)
rate.exposure: Drug concentration measured after death in blood from different vessels and in other specimens, and at different times after death
rate.comparator: Femoral (thigh vein) blood from the same body; a blood sample taken in life (one case); earlier samples from the same body
rate.outcome: Size and direction of differences in measured drug concentration between sampling sites and over time after death
rate.magnitude: Within one body (four selected overdoses, autopsy about 7 to 48 h after death): highest to lowest systemic-blood value 3.5- to 6.6-fold (excluding the separately reported portal values) per drug taken in the overdose (editors' calculation; doxepin 3.5, amobarbital 6.0, secobarbital 6.5, pentobarbital 6.2, clomipramine 5.4, flurazepam 6.6, imipramine 4.4; lidocaine given in hospital 1.6). One case with a sample from life: post-mortem imipramine 4.1–18.1 mg/L against 2.3 mg/L in hospital, 1.8- to 7.9-fold. Medians across drug-specific medians of paired within-case ratios (printed number of results): other blood 1.27 (576), muscle 0.99 (385), vitreous humour 0.45 (356), brain 1.84 (565), heart 2.03 (185), kidney 2.86 (401), lung 3.69 (187), spleen 4.25 (71), liver 5.06 (1,697), bile 5.52 (537); between drugs, liver 0.95–54.29, vitreous 0.03–1.59, other blood 0.90–14.61; other blood for morphine 1.26 (53), methamphetamine 1.50 (9). Human repeated sampling: first sample on average 17 h after death (range 1–292 h) where reported or estimated; rises in femoral blood for about 12 drugs, falls for 5 (no sizes). Narrative-review approximate heart-to-peripheral values without case counts or per-value sources (82 numeric-labelled entries among 98 distinct labels, including a nicotine/cotinine annotation; two ranges): morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5–2.3; more than 10% above the compilation's paired other-blood median for 17 of 24 drugs in both (editors' comparison). No within-drug intervals are given. The Table 3 N columns sum to 4,960 but include one oxazepam brain count without a printed ratio; the counts are results, not distinct deaths.
rate.short: Yes. Levels can rise or fall after death and differ between blood vessels, so a drug can look more or less involved in a death than it was.
rate.rate: Different kinds of study agree that levels change. But the evidence is four deaths picked as examples, 5,375 cases gathered mostly from published reports without a quality check, and reviews mostly about medicines.

risk_of_bias.note: Seen only through one brief meta-analysis that did not appraise its studies (METHODS §6.3, not appraisable): it pooled experimental and quasi-experimental evaluations without saying which were which, entered four of the 11 effects (39% of the students listed) as assumed zeros, and ignored the clustering of students in schools, which makes its interval too narrow (card sc_west_2004: AMSTAR 2, critically low confidence). The biases expected in non-randomized school comparisons and in self-reported use would, if anything, favour D.A.R.E., so they do not point to a hidden benefit.

inconsistency.note: Study estimates vary more than chance would predict (I² about 54%, editors' calculation), but most intervals include zero, the two studies that found less use are the smallest (one measured only smoking) and the largest found slightly more use with D.A.R.E.; the variation does not show a setting in which the original curriculum clearly worked, and the near-zero result holds under fixed- and random-effects pooling (editors' recalculation).

indirectness.note: Worded for the original curriculum in schools (studies published 1991–2002; no country given, though the review presents D.A.R.E. as a US programme) and for alcohol, tobacco and illegal drug use combined; no result for a single substance is given, and the claim does not apply to the curriculum revised in 2001.

imprecision.note: The pooled interval (−0.04 to 0.08) excludes effects as large as Cohen's small benchmark; that it is too narrow because clustering was ignored is counted under risk of bias, not twice.

publication_bias.note: Journal articles only; unpublished null evaluations would not change a null result, and the earlier meta-analysis that included agency reports also found negligible effects, as described.

rate.reasoning: The review admitted experimental and quasi-experimental designs without saying which studies were randomized, so the evidence cannot be treated as randomized and starts low; seen only through this review, which did not appraise its studies, it is rated down one level for risk of bias (METHODS §6.3), giving very low, the floor. Rated as worded: no detectable effect of the original curriculum on self-reported use of alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs combined; the pooled effect is near zero (d = 0.023) with an interval that excludes Cohen's small benchmark, and a fixed-effect pooling gives −0.005 (editors' recalculation). The very low rating reflects how little this single brief review lets anyone check (designs not reported, four effects assumed, clustering ignored), not a sign of a hidden benefit: the biases expected in such studies would favour D.A.R.E. The authors' remark that the effect would need to be 20 times larger to count as small is not adopted (about 9 times, editors' calculation). Status replicated: the review reports each study's direction, and in 8 of 11 independent evaluations the interval included no difference; the earlier meta-analysis, described in the paper but not read, agrees and is not counted. The answer does not cover the curriculum revised in 2001.
rate.population: School students in grades 5 to 12 (no country given in the review, which presents D.A.R.E. as a US programme; 236 to 2,878 per study; 11,505 listed across the 11 studies, editors' sum) in 11 controlled evaluations (experimental or quasi-experimental, not distinguished in the review) published in peer-reviewed journals from 1991 to 2002
rate.exposure: The original Project D.A.R.E. school curriculum, before its 2001 revision; content, number of sessions and delivery not described in the review
rate.comparator: Each study's control or comparison condition, not described in the review
rate.outcome: Self-reported use of alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs, combined into one effect per study, from immediately after the programme to 10 years later
rate.magnitude: West & O'Neal (2004): pooled r = 0.011, d = 0.023 (95% CI −0.04 to 0.08; the interval is on the d scale, editors' check), z = 0.73, not significant; positive values favour D.A.R.E. Study effects (Table 1): Becker 1992 d = −0.117 (−0.19 to −0.04; 2,878 students); Zagumny & Thompson 1997 d = 0.376 (0.07 to 0.68; 395); Ahmed 2002 d = 0.405 (0.01 to 0.80; 236; smoking only); four effects entered as assumed zeros (Ennett 1994, Rosenbaum 1994, Wysong 1994, Lynam 1999; 4,539 of 11,505 students, 39%, editors' sum); 8 of 11 intervals include zero (editors' count). Editors' recalculation from the printed d values and intervals: random-effects (DerSimonian–Laird) d = 0.023 (−0.039 to 0.085), reproducing the published estimate; fixed-effect d = −0.005 (−0.043 to 0.034); Q = 21.6 on 10 df (P about 0.02), I² about 54%. Cohen's small benchmarks (d = 0.2, r = 0.1) are about 8.7 and 9.1 times the pooled values (editors' calculation), against the paper's 20 times. No absolute difference in the share of students using any substance can be given.
rate.short: No. Across 11 studies of the original DARE school classes, kids who had DARE used alcohol, tobacco and other drugs about as much as kids who didn't.
rate.rate: One short review that didn't check how well its 11 studies were done, and filled in four results as zero. That's no hint of a hidden benefit: the biases expected in such studies would favour DARE.

lines.statement: In about 15,000 written reports of drug experiences on the Erowid website, covering 165 substances (reports of combinations left out; all reports for each substance merged into one document; drug names, slang and words for routes deleted), compared with 625 written accounts of near-death experiences that people gave voluntarily to research groups in the USA and Belgium (also merged into one document), reports about ketamine, compared with the reports about each of the other 164 substances, are associated with the pattern of word use most similar to the near-death accounts, as scored by a text-mining method (latent semantic analysis) that gives one similarity number per substance, with no measure of uncertainty and no check against questionnaires about experiences (Martial et al., 2019). Nobody was given a drug or interviewed for this study. With the main settings (20 dimensions), ketamine scored about 0.90 on a 0-to-1 scale, against about 0.84 for Salvia divinorum and about 0.83 for peyote and for LSD (values the editors read from a figure); averaged over all the settings tried (5 to 145 dimensions), ketamine led narrowly, about 0.64 against about 0.61 for LSD and about 0.60 for psilocybin mushrooms, and it came first with about 4 in 5 of the settings (read from a pie chart), LSD with most of the rest. Rankings made with very different settings agreed poorly below the top: peyote, third with the main settings, was about 18th on the average. When the near-death accounts were split by cause, closeness to death or how pleasant they were, ketamine stayed first in almost every subset; after cardiac arrest, LSD ranked comparably. As classes, dissociative drugs ranked first, then deliriants and serotonergic psychedelics, with sedatives, stimulants and antipsychotics or antidepressants lowest. Similar word patterns are not shown to be similar experiences: the score counts how words occur together (a word such as fear counts whether it was felt or denied, as the authors note); the near-death accounts were written on average about two decades after the event, and 30% were attributed to anaesthesia or drug use (cause missing for 228 of 625; the base of the percentage is not stated); the Erowid writers, their doses and settings are unknown and the substances were not tested; and the authors state that their analysis neither validates nor refutes neurochemical explanations of near-death experiences, such as the idea that the brain releases a ketamine-like chemical near death, although their abstract says the results support that speculation and suggests ketamine could be a safe and reversible experimental model of near-death experiences, which was not studied. Funded by public research bodies and private foundations; two of the 12 authors are at the Erowid Center, which curates the reports; no conflict-of-interest statement is printed. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Two existing collections of written reports, merged by substance: (1) about 15,000 reports from the Erowid Experience Vaults, a curated website holding more than 20,000 reports written by people who chose to submit them, on 165 substances with more than 10 single-substance reports each (demographic information on the writers not commonly available; the authors call the population relatively homogeneous culturally; doses and settings unknown); (2) 625 retrospective narratives (623,926 words) of near-death experiences given in an anonymous voluntary questionnaire to the Division of Perceptual Studies, University of Virginia Health System (USA), and the Coma Science Group, University and University Hospital of Liège (Belgium), all scoring 7 or more on the NDE Scale except 182 collected before the scale existed; 68% women; mean age 31 (SD 15) at the experience and 52 (SD 13) when the account was collected; cause attributed to head injury 13%, anaesthesia or drug use 30%, cardiac arrest 10% (228 missing)
lines.exposure: Reports about ketamine, as named by their writers (substance, dose and route not verified; route words deleted from the texts)
lines.comparator: Reports about each of the other 164 substances, ranked against one another; no collection of other kinds of experience was compared
lines.outcome: Similarity of word use between each substance's merged reports and the merged near-death accounts: the correlation of reduced term-document columns after tf-idf weighting and latent semantic analysis (20 singular values in the main analysis, 5 to 145 in robustness checks); the resulting ranking of substances and of drug classes
lines.magnitude: Martial et al. (2019) print no values, intervals or tests for the ranking itself. Main analysis (20 singular values; Fig. 3, editors' measurement of dot centres at 600 dpi, approximate): ketamine 0.90, Salvia divinorum 0.84, Lophophora williamsii (peyote) 0.83, LSD 0.83, 5-MeO-DMT 0.83, psilocybin mushrooms 0.82, DMT 0.82; Datura species (21st in the zoomed panel) 0.72; betel nut (lowest) about 0.08. Mean over 5 to 145 singular values (Fig. 7C, editors' measurement of bar tops at 600 dpi, approximate): ketamine 0.64, LSD 0.61, psilocybin mushrooms 0.60, S. divinorum 0.59, cannabis 0.59; L. williamsii 18th. Ketamine first in about 79% of the settings, LSD about 13%, ibogaine about 6%, L. williamsii about 1% and PCP under 1% (Fig. 7D; editors' measurement of the slice angles, approximate; no shares printed). After deleting the 500 most relevant terms of each of two context topics (20 singular values): top ten ketamine, ayahuasca, S. divinorum, L. williamsii, 5-MeO-DMT, LSD, cannabis, psilocybin mushrooms, iboga, nitrous oxide. By class (Fig. 4): dissociatives first, then deliriants and serotonergic psychedelics; dissociatives differed from every class except deliriants (pairwise tests at p < 0.05, 12 of 21 pairs marked significant, editors' count; no correction reported). NDE subsets: ketamine first in almost all; LSD comparable after cardiac arrest.
lines.reasoning: Observational evidence (a cross-sectional text analysis of two existing collections of written reports) starts low; rated down two levels for risk of bias and one for imprecision, it is very low, the floor. Rated as worded: an association between the substance a report names and how closely its pooled word use resembles pooled near-death accounts, in these two self-selected collections. The claim does not say that ketamine produces an experience like a near-death experience, that near-death experiences have a ketamine-like chemical cause, or that ketamine is a safe experimental model: the abstract's and conclusion's statements to that effect are not adopted, because safety was not studied and the discussion itself says the analysis neither validates nor refutes neurochemical models (p. 65). What the design cannot show is said in the statement: word co-occurrence is not experience, the near-death accounts were written about two decades after the events and some followed anaesthesia or drug use, and nothing about the Erowid writers or their doses is known. 'Is associated with' because the design is observational and the certainty very low (METHODS §6.1). Values are the editors' readings of figures that print none, labelled as approximate. Status single study.

lines.q: Do people describe ketamine trips the way others describe near-death experiences?
lines.short: More than for any other drug, going by the words alone: of 165 drugs, ketamine trip reports read most like near-death accounts. Salvia and LSD came close behind.
lines.but: Only words were compared. Nobody showed the trips and the near-death experiences feel alike.
how: Researchers took about 15,000 drug reports from the Erowid website. A computer compared their words with 625 near-death accounts.
Ketamine came first with the main settings, and with about 4 in 5 of all the settings tried. On average it led LSD only narrowly, and lower down, drugs swapped places.
The near-death accounts were written about 20 years after the event, on average, and some were linked to anaesthesia or drug use. Nobody checked what the online writers took, or how much.
Some think the brain releases a ketamine-like chemical near death. The authors say their study can't show that, though their summary says it supports the idea.
lines.q_on_site_now: Do people describe ketamine trips the way others describe near-death experiences?

lines.statement: In the clinical trials of MDMA-assisted therapy reviewed up to 2024, almost all in PTSD (outside PTSD, one randomized trial each in 12 autistic adults with social anxiety and in 18 people with anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, plus small open-label studies and a case series), MDMA compared with placebo or low-dose MDMA increased common side effects during sessions and in the following week, such as jaw clenching or muscle tightness, anxiety, reduced appetite, nausea, sweating, feeling cold and headache, which the reviews describe as mostly mild to moderate and largely transient. A 2024 meta-analysis found higher odds of any expected reaction during sessions in phase 2 trials (odds ratio 1.67, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.49) and of any treatment-emergent adverse event in the two phase 3 trials (3.51, 2.76 to 4.46), although its any-event percentages cannot be shares of participants; in the life-threatening-illness trial, jaw clenching occurred in 11 of 13 people on MDMA and 1 of 5 on placebo. The meta-analysis found no difference in psychiatric adverse events (phase 2), in suicidality or cardiac events of special interest (phase 3) or in dropping out, and a network meta-analysis found no excess of severe adverse events; a 2022 review found one serious adverse event related to MDMA in the studies it covered (more frequent premature heartbeats, present before treatment, needing a night of hospital monitoring). The record of harms is weak: most studies relied on spontaneous reports, no trial reported harms adequately by the CONSORT Harms 2022 standard, 56% of the non-serious and 4 of the 13 serious adverse events listed in the trial registries were missing from the publications (the 4 all in MDMA groups), and the meta-analysis found too little data on risks beyond active treatment, from small and highly selected samples. Certainty: low (for the increase in common side effects). Status: replicated by the same team.
lines.population: People treated in clinical trials of MDMA-assisted therapy: mostly adults with PTSD; also autistic adults with social anxiety, people with anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, people with alcohol use disorder (open-label) and couples in which one partner has PTSD
lines.exposure: MDMA in one to three sessions within psychotherapy
lines.comparator: Inactive placebo or low-dose MDMA with the same psychotherapy
lines.outcome: Side effects and adverse events during and after treatment, serious adverse events, adverse events of special interest, withdrawal, and completeness of harms reporting
lines.magnitude: Colcott 2024 (8 randomized trials, 298 participants, in the meta-analyses; 13 studies, 333 participants, in the review): phase 2, any expected reaction during sessions OR 1.67 (1.12 to 2.49), 45% against 30%; in the following 7 days OR 1.59 (1.12 to 2.24), 46% against 31%; anxiety OR 4.84 and jaw clenching OR 4.72 during sessions (Fig. 2; the Discussion prints the two the other way round); phase 3, any TEAE OR 3.51 (2.76 to 4.46), 16% against 5% (unit unclear), 13 named TEAEs more frequent; no difference in phase 2 TEAEs or psychiatric TEAEs, phase 3 suicidality or cardiac AESIs, or withdrawal. Registers against publications: 1487 against 661 non-serious events (5 trials), 13 against 9 serious events (8 trials). Life-threatening illness trial (Schipper 2024, Table 4): jaw clenching 11/13 (84.6%) against 1/5 (20.0%), thirst 11/13 against 2/5, perspiration 9/13 against 0/5; no treatment-related serious adverse events. Autistic adults (Breeksema 2022, Table 1): acute anxiety 6/8 against 1/4.
lines.reasoning: Randomized comparisons start high. Rated down once for risk of bias (spontaneous, probably unblinded recording) and once for indirectness (a claim across indications resting mostly on PTSD trials of one sponsor, seen through systematic reviews). Certainty applies to the increase in common side effects; rare, serious or delayed harms cannot be assessed from these trials, which the claim says. The causal verb is used because the comparisons are randomized and the effects are those expected pharmacologically, although the reviews themselves describe them as associations. Most trials share the sponsor and protocol, hence replicated by the same team. This overlaps the phase 3 adverse-event claim in this section, which rests on the trial reports read directly.

lines.q: What side effects does MDMA cause in therapy trials?
lines.short: Common ones were a tight jaw, anxiety, less appetite, feeling sick and sweating. They happened during sessions and in the week after. Most were mild to moderate and soon passed.
lines.but: The record is patchy. Most studies only noted problems people raised themselves. Some never reached the papers, and later risks are barely known.
how: These effects were more common than with a dummy pill or a very small dose.
In one small trial in people with a serious illness, 11 of 13 on MDMA had a tight jaw, against 1 of 5 on a dummy pill.
One review found one serious problem linked to MDMA. Extra heartbeats the person already had got more frequent. They were watched overnight in hospital.
Trial records listed problems the papers left out. That was more than half of the less serious ones, and 4 of 13 serious ones. All 4 were in people on MDMA.
lines.q_on_site_now: Across all MDMA therapy trials, which side effects were common?

lines.statement: As described second-hand by two narrative reviews (no primary study of this was read), tolerance to opioids is thought to fall during a period without them, so that a dose that was once usual may have a much greater effect, including on breathing, when use starts again. Neither review gives an estimate, so the evidence is insufficient to say how long a break must last, how fast tolerance falls, or by how much the chance of a fatal overdose rises. White and Irvine (1999) offer the idea as a possible explanation and rest it on one hair-analysis study (less morphine in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using, which they read as a sign of lower use before death); they say that information on the rate of loss is sparse and that the loss may be quick and uneven between effects, and they describe two studies in people on methadone maintenance that found tolerance to the breathing-depressing effect of methadone to be incomplete. Hickman et al. (2008) say, citing White and Irvine, that risk appears to be raised after periods of relative abstinence, for example following incarceration or detoxification; White and Irvine write of a period of abstinence, and separately of treatment with naltrexone, and do not name either of those settings.
lines.population: People who use opioids (heroin, methadone and other opioids), as described in two narrative reviews; no primary study of a break from opioids was read
lines.exposure: A period without opioids (a period of abstinence in the reviews' wording) before use starts again
lines.comparator: Continued regular use; the same person's tolerance before the break
lines.outcome: Tolerance to opioid effects, including breathing depression, and the chance of a fatal overdose when use starts again
lines.magnitude: No estimate in either source. White and Irvine (1999), second-hand: one hair-analysis study (Tagliaro et al., 1998) found lower morphine content in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using (no numbers given in the review); the rate of loss of tolerance for euphoric, analgesic and respiratory effects is called sparse, probably uneven and possibly quick (receptor changes can occur in minutes or hours); incomplete tolerance to the breathing-depressing effect of methadone in two studies of people on methadone maintenance (Marks and Goldring, 1973; Santiago et al., 1977; no numbers given). Hickman et al. (2008): risk appears to be raised after periods of relative abstinence; no figures.
lines.reasoning: A claim seen only through reviews starts from the design of the primary studies they describe, here observational (a hair-analysis comparison of people who died of overdose with people who were still using) and human studies of methadone, so it starts low, and is downgraded for risk of bias (primary studies not appraisable) and for indirectness (second-hand; one review cites the other). Certainty very low. The relation is insufficient evidence because neither source gives a size, a time course or a risk figure. Because every supporting anchor is a narrative review, the claim stays at draft and says so in its statement (METHODS 6.3). Status: single study in effect (Hickman et al. rest on White and Irvine for this point). The claim keeps to what the text says: White and Irvine name only a period of abstinence, and the examples of incarceration and detoxification belong to Hickman et al.

lines.q: Why can the usual amount be dangerous after a break?
lines.short: Tolerance may drop during a break from opioids, two reviews say. So the usual amount may hit much harder, breathing included.
lines.but: The reviews give no numbers. Not how long a break must be, or how much the risk of a fatal overdose rises.
how: The older review offers this as a possible explanation. It says tolerance may fade quickly, and not at the same pace for every effect. But there's little data on how fast.
The idea rests on one hair study. People who died of heroin overdose had less morphine in their hair than people still using. The review reads that as less use before death.
The newer review gives prison and detox as examples of a break; the older one, which it cites, doesn't.
Two studies of people on methadone found tolerance to its effect on breathing was not complete.
lines.q_on_site_now: Why can the usual amount be dangerous after a break?

lines.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music changes how a ketamine or esketamine session feels or how well the treatment works; one randomized trial found a smaller rise in blood pressure with music. In that trial (Greenway et al., 2024; Montreal, 2021 to 2022; registered), 32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression, accepted for a clinical course of six intravenous ketamine infusions over 4 weeks (treatment conditions), were randomly assigned to curated music throughout each 40-minute infusion (15) or to usual care without music (17). Across 181 infusions, systolic blood pressure rose from the start to the end of each infusion by 7.4 mm Hg less with music than without (95% CI 2.9 to 12.0; a mean rise of roughly 11.5 against 18.5 mm Hg, read from the figure), while diastolic pressure did not differ detectably (0.8 mm Hg less; the printed interval, −1.59 to 3.18, appears to have its signs transposed); no serious adverse events were recorded. The letter reports nothing on how the sessions felt, dissociation or depression (it says that its secondary outcomes, which it does not name, will be published elsewhere), nor how many patients in each group needed treatment for raised blood pressure (citing an expert review, the authors say that up to 20% of patients given intravenous ketamine for treatment-resistant depression need such treatment); the comparison was with no music, without a sound or attention control, so the music cannot be separated from attention or expectation; and one patient given usual care was left out of the analysis without a stated reason. Before that trial, as described in one scoping review (Kheirkhah et al., 2024; searched to December 2023; the included studies were not appraised, so its figures are second-hand), 14 studies of music with ketamine had been published, all in patients in clinical or trial settings. In nine, ketamine was given with other sedatives or painkillers, during procedures or, in one study, air medical transport; in most of them music went with less sedation or drug use and lower anxiety, pain or fear, but one trial found no effect on emergence reactions and another found more dreams or emergence reactions with music, though no unpleasant dreams, against 10 controls with unpleasant dreams. Of the five studies of ketamine or esketamine alone, only one compared people who listened with people who heard nothing: in 46 children having heart catheterization under ketamine anaesthesia, the 23 who heard recordings of their mothers' voices (musical in 12 of them) had less anxiety before the procedure and fewer emergence reactions than 23 who wore headphones with no recording. The other four were case reports and interview studies without such a comparison: a woman on esketamine nasal spray found that music of her choice helped with dissociation, confusion and anxiety; two patients with bipolar depression tolerated dissociation better with preferred music in later infusions, which may reflect getting used to the infusions; in 12 people given ketamine in a trial for alcohol use disorder, everyone who listened to music heard it distorted in speed and pitch, felt as good or bad depending on their state; and in 17 people on oral esketamine for depression, music was described as blocking distractions and helping inner exploration, but some felt it kept them tied to the outside world and one stopped using it. Up to its search, the review found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine or esketamine treatment for depression, and its own limitations say no conclusions can be drawn. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: 32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression receiving a clinical course of intravenous ketamine in Montreal (one randomized trial), and patients given ketamine or esketamine in clinical settings (anaesthesia, sedation, depression and alcohol-use-disorder treatment) in 14 earlier studies gathered by a scoping review
lines.exposure: Curated music throughout each 40-minute ketamine infusion (trial); music (or, in one study, recordings of mothers' voices) before, during or after ketamine or esketamine (review)
lines.comparator: Usual care without music (trial); no music (headphones with no recording, or a blank soundtrack) in most procedural trials and in the one comparison of ketamine alone; no comparison in the case reports and interview studies (review)
lines.outcome: Rise in systolic and diastolic blood pressure from the start to the end of each infusion (trial); anxiety, pain, emergence reactions, sedative use, dissociation and how the session was experienced (review)
lines.magnitude: Greenway et al. (2024), randomized, 181 infusions in 32 patients (31 apparently analysed for the primary outcome, editors' inference from the flow diagram): change in systolic blood pressure from 0 to 40 minutes, music against no music, β −7.4 mm Hg (95% CI −12.0 to −2.9), P = .008; diastolic β −0.8 mm Hg (printed 95% CI −1.59 to 3.18, an interval centred on +0.8, so its signs appear transposed), P = .58; read approximately from the figure, mean systolic rise about 11.5 mm Hg with music and 18.5 mm Hg without; no clinical, experience or depression outcome reported. Kheirkhah et al. (2024): no pooled estimates. 14 studies: 9 with other sedatives (music with less sedation and lower anxiety or pain in most; no effect on emergence reactions in one; more dreams or emergence reactions in another); 5 with ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparing listeners with children who heard nothing (46 children: mothers' voices against headphones with no recording), the rest case reports (3 patients) and interview studies (17 and 12 people). No study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression up to December 2023.
lines.reasoning: The best evidence is now one randomized trial, which starts high, but it answers only blood pressure: on its own, the smaller systolic rise with music would rate low (high, minus one for risk of bias and one for imprecision). For how a session feels, the evidence is still the review's small, mostly procedural studies seen second-hand (low, minus risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low). Rated for the claim as worded: down one each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, giving very low. Status single study: one randomized trial for blood pressure, and, for ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparison of listening with not listening (46 children under anaesthesia hearing recordings of their mothers' voices), seen through one review. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3), and every anchor has been checked by a second reader. The trial's secondary outcomes, deferred to later publications, have not been seen.

lines.q: Does music change how a ketamine treatment session goes?
lines.short: Nobody knows yet whether it changes how a session feels or how well ketamine works. One trial found the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less with music.
lines.but: Just 32 patients; the report gave no results on how the sessions felt.
how: 32 patients with hard-to-treat depression were starting a course of six ketamine drips. Chance decided who heard music during each drip; the rest heard none.
With music, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less during each drip. The bottom number didn't clearly differ.
Before that, a review found 14 studies of music with ketamine. In most, ketamine came with other drugs during medical procedures. None compared music with no music in treating depression.
The review's case reports and interviews had no comparison. Some said music eased the detached feeling or blocked distractions; others heard it warped, or felt it kept them tied to the outside world.
lines.q_on_site_now: Does music change how a ketamine treatment session goes?

lines.statement: In people who had used LSD in the past 12 months and took part in the Global Drug Survey 2017, an anonymous online survey of drug use open from November 2016 to January 2017 in 10 languages, which people chose to join through social networks, media partners and harm-reduction organisations and were not paid for (13,769 respondents reported past-year use: 63.9% were under 25, 79.6% men, and most lived in Germany, the USA, the UK, Denmark, Canada or Australia), 102 of the 10,293 who answered the question (1.0%; about 1 in 100, or 10 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency medical treatment after LSD in that year (Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al., 2022). The denominator is the people who answered that question (75% of those reporting past-year use, editors' calculation), not everyone who reported past-year use, although the abstract describes the 10,293 as the past-year group. Emergency treatment was not defined, answers were not checked against any record, nothing that was taken was tested, and the number of incidents per person was not asked; dividing the 102 people by an estimated 53,627 days of use (a mean of 5.21 days a year), the authors put the figure at 0.2% of past-year uses, which they call an underestimate because each person is counted once. In the companion analysis of the same survey, 19 of 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year and answered (0.2%; about 2 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency treatment after them, a share the authors describe as about five times lower (Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al., 2022). Saying yes was more common among people with a lifetime mental health diagnosis (1.8% against 0.7%; χ2(1, N = 8,299) = 19.33, p < 0.001), among younger people (median age 21 against 22; p = 0.003) and among those with more days of use in the past year (median 3 against 2; p = 0.029), in separate tests without adjustment, and it did not differ by sex or by first use in the past year. Of the 102, most ticked anxiety or panic (71) and confusion (66), and many paranoia (50) or seeing or hearing things (46); 21 (20.6%) ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm, 17 (16.7%) an accident or trauma, 13 (12.7%) seizures and 12 (11.8%) passing out, none of it verified, and the authors say it is unknown which symptoms came from LSD and which from other drugs taken. 54.5% said they had been admitted to hospital, a share the authors call surprising and print without a count, noting that the survey did not define admission. The paper gives recovery as percentages without a denominator, 59.2% back to normal within 24 hours and 11.2% with consequences lasting beyond 4 weeks; both fit 98 respondents, and the editors' reading of the figure, which prints no values, gives 58 of 98 back to normal within 24 hours, 40 taking longer, 17 not back to normal after 5 to 7 days and 11 with problems beyond 4 weeks, 6 of whom said they had not recovered (the abstract gives the 11). In the session that led to emergency treatment, 33 of the 102 had taken nothing else and 69 (editors' subtraction) had also taken another substance, most often cannabis (51) or alcohol (24); how often people combined substances in sessions that did not end in emergency treatment was not asked. Choosing up to three of six reasons, 53.9% named the setting, 50.0% their mindset, 40.2% taking too much and 34.3% mixing with other drugs; about 13 of the 102 thought the drug had not been LSD and about 10 did not know (both read by the editors from a figure that prints no values). Afterwards, 62.7% said they had cut down their LSD use and 16.7% that it had not changed. The authors cite similar shares in later rounds of the same survey (0.9%, 1.0% and 0.8% in the 2019, 2020 and 2021 rounds; those reports were not read here); they write that the incidents captured are likely only a proportion of LSD-related adverse events, most likely the more severe ones, that some serious reactions may not lead to emergency treatment (for example from fear of legal consequences), that some visits may be false alarms raised by others, and that drugs mistaken for LSD, such as NBOMes, may account for some incidents. They read their results as showing LSD to be relatively safe when used recreationally, with adverse reactions 'typically short-lived, self-limiting and psychological in nature', while their own figures show 40 of 98 taking longer than a day and 21 of 102 reporting thoughts or acts of self-harm; the survey cannot count deaths or people who could not or did not answer. The survey's founder and owner is an author; King's College London receives funding from COMPASS Pathways for psilocybin trials led by two of the authors, one of whom (Rucker) has been paid as a consultant by Clerkenwell Health and Beckley PsyTech, and the other (Young) has had honoraria and consulting fees from several drug companies and co-edits the publishing journal; the funding statement names UK National Institute for Health Research support for those two authors and no funder for the survey. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Respondents to the Global Drug Survey 2017 (anonymous, online, self-nominated; November 2016 to January 2017; 10 languages) who reported LSD use in the past 12 months (13,769; 63.9% under 25, 79.6% men, most living in Germany, the USA, the UK, Denmark, Canada or Australia), of whom 10,293 answered the emergency-treatment question
lines.exposure: Use of LSD in the past 12 months, self-reported; nothing tested, so what was taken is not confirmed; other substances in the incident session as reported
lines.comparator: None outside the sample: within it, respondents who answered and did not report seeking emergency treatment (for age, sex, mental health diagnosis, first use, doses per day of use and frequency of use); in the companion analysis of the same survey, respondents who had used magic mushrooms
lines.outcome: Self-reported seeking of emergency medical treatment (not defined) after LSD in the past 12 months; for those who said yes, symptoms ticked from a list of 20, self-reported hospital admission (not defined), time to feel back to normal, other substances in that session, perceived reasons and change in use
lines.magnitude: Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al. (2022): 102 of 10,293 who answered (1.0%; editors' Wilson 95% interval 0.82% to 1.20%); per day of use 0.001902 (0.2%; 102 divided by an estimated 53,627 days; an underestimate by the authors' account). Lifetime mental health diagnosis 1.8% against 0.7% (χ2(1, N = 8,299) = 19.33, p < 0.001); median age 21 against 22 (p = 0.003); median days of use 3 against 2 (p = 0.029). Of the 102: anxiety or panic 71, confusion 66, paranoia 50, seeing or hearing things 46, thoughts or acts of self-harm 21 (20.6%), accident or trauma 17 (16.7%), seizures 13 (12.7%), passing out 12 (11.8%); hospital admission 54.5% (no count; not defined); back to normal within 24 hours 59.2% and consequences beyond 4 weeks 11.2% (58 and 11 of 98 by the editors' reading; 40 of 98 longer than 24 hours, 17 longer than 5 to 7 days, 6 not recovered); nothing else taken 33, cannabis 51, alcohol 24; reasons setting 53.9%, mindset 50.0%, too much 40.2%, mixing 34.3%, not LSD about 13 of 102 and don't know about 10 (figure, editors' reading). Companion magic mushroom analysis (Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al., 2022): 19 of 9,233 (0.2%), about five times lower by the authors' account.
lines.reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the population sampled (METHODS §6.3): starts low; down one for measurement (risk of bias) and one for coverage (indirectness), giving very low, the floor; never upgraded. 'Describes' because it reports how many respondents said they had sought emergency treatment, not a risk for people who use LSD and not a cause of the symptoms. The associations with mental health diagnosis, age and frequency are univariate and are reported as associations among respondents. The question is worded with 'seek', not 'need', because the survey asked whether people had sought emergency treatment, not whether they needed it, and the authors themselves say that some who needed treatment may not have sought it while some visits may have been false alarms. Status single study: one survey wave; the later rounds the authors cite come from the same survey programme and team and were not read, and the magic mushroom figure is a companion analysis of the same survey, so neither counts as replication. The authors' conclusion that reactions are typically short-lived and self-limiting is not adopted, because their own recovery and symptom figures qualify it. Numbers of doses are left out, and 'taking too much' appears only as a reason respondents chose.

lines.q: How often do people seek emergency treatment after LSD?
lines.short: About 10 in 1,000 people who had used LSD in the past year said they sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After magic mushrooms: 2 in 1,000.
lines.but: Volunteers took an online survey about themselves. Nobody checked their answers, or if the drug was really LSD.
how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 10,293 people who had used LSD in the past year answered this question; 102 said yes.
Most of the 102 ticked panic, anxiety or confusion. 21 ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm. About half said they were admitted to hospital.
Of about 98 who said how long it lasted, 58 felt back to normal within a day, 40 took longer, and 11 still had problems after 4 weeks.
People with a past mental health diagnosis reported seeking emergency treatment more often: 1.8 in 100, against 0.7 in 100.
lines.q_on_site_now: How often do people seek emergency treatment after LSD?

lines.statement: In bodies examined after death, the measured concentration of a drug in blood can differ from the concentration at the moment of death, and from one blood vessel to another in the same body, by amounts that vary between drugs and between bodies and that, in the sources read, cannot yet be predicted for a given death. In four suspected overdose deaths chosen by forensic medicine authors in Dundee and Edmonton to illustrate the problem (tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and the sleeping medicine flurazepam; autopsy about 7 to 48 hours after death; office and period not stated), blood drawn separately from up to 11 systemic vessels of the same body differed 3.5- to 6.6-fold for each drug taken in the overdose and 1.6-fold for lidocaine, given in hospital (editors' calculation from the printed ranges), usually highest in central vessels near the lungs and liver and lowest in the subclavian or femoral veins, though in one case the lowest value was in the pulmonary artery; in the only person with a blood sample from life, taken in hospital about one hour before cardiac arrest (the reported intervals imply about two hours before death), every post-mortem sample, femoral blood included, held 1.8 to 7.9 times as much imipramine (editors' calculation). The authors attribute the differences mainly to drug diffusing out of organs after death, while allowing incomplete distribution in life as a contributor and calling the cause unresolved and probably multifactorial; the report describes one post-mortem sampling occasion per body, alongside the separate sample from life in case 4 and unabsorbed drug was still in the gut in three of the four, so part of the differences may have arisen before death (Pounder & Jones, 1990). A compilation of 10,993 results from 5,375 post-mortem cases for 50 compounds (published reports found by keyword searching, plus a Finnish national laboratory database for 2000 to 2018; cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids were left out) calculated within-case ratios where a published source gave both values, then medians for each drug; the medians across these drug-specific medians were 1.27 for other blood such as heart blood (576 results), 0.99 for muscle, 0.45 for the fluid of the eye (vitreous humour), 1.84 for brain, 2.03 for heart muscle, 5.06 for liver and 5.52 for bile, with more than tenfold ranges across the available drug-specific medians in all ten specimen types (other blood from 0.90 to 14.61, vitreous humour from 0.03 to 1.59, liver from 0.95 to 54.29, some of these values resting on few results; for other blood, morphine 1.26 and methamphetamine 1.50); no within-drug range or interval is given, and cause of death and time since death, which the sources did not always give, could not be taken into account (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019). A review of 87 publications selected from a two-database search in April 2025 reports that in animal experiments drug levels in heart blood rose within minutes of death; that in human bodies sampled more than once, femoral blood, the sample thought least open to change (Ferner, 2008), rose significantly after death for about a dozen drugs, among them fentanyl and methadone, and fell for others, among them 6-MAM (the marker of heroin) and THC; and that, in the studies that reported or estimated it, the reported mean time to the first sample was about 17 hours after death (range 1 to 292 hours), so change before then was not seen. That summary is accompanied by 12 citations, but the review does not supply the underlying interval values, weights or aggregation method. It gives no sizes and does not appraise the studies; it judges that a heart-to-femoral blood ratio other than 1 can indicate, if the two were equal at death, that change after death occurred but not how much, and that a ratio of 1 does not rule it out, and it concludes that evidence linking the change to specific variables is often lacking, drug properties explaining only part of it (Borra et al., 2026). A 2003 practitioners' review lists 99 entries (98 distinct labels), of which 82 have numeric parentheses, including an ambiguous nicotine/cotinine annotation; two are ranges and 16 labels, including THC, have no numeric value. It gives no case counts or per-value source attribution (for example morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3); for 17 of 24 shared labels its value exceeds 1.10 times the compilation's paired median for other blood. Other blood is not only heart blood, and the review's peripheral blood is not necessarily femoral; this comparison is descriptive, not a validated correction (editors' comparison; Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ketola & Kriikku, 2019), and a clinical pharmacologist's review adds that post-mortem whole blood is compared with plasma or serum values from living patients, and that the ratio between the two differs by drug even in life (Ferner, 2008). Change can run both ways: a level after death can be higher than in life, as in the one case with a hospital sample, which can make a drug look more involved in a death than it was, or it can fall after death, as reported for 6-MAM and THC, which can make a drug look less involved. The evidence consists of a selected case series, an unappraised compilation drawn mostly from published reports, some of them about poisonings, and narrative reviews, mostly about medicines; how often, and by how much, a level changes in an ordinary death is not known. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: Bodies examined after death: four selected suspected overdose deaths at medico-legal autopsy (Pounder & Jones, 1990); 5,375 post-mortem cases from published reports and a Finnish laboratory database, 2000 to 2018 (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019); animal experiments and human bodies sampled more than once, as reviewed (Borra et al., 2026); narrative reviews (Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ferner, 2008)
lines.exposure: Drug concentration measured after death in blood from different vessels and in other specimens, and at different times after death
lines.comparator: Femoral (thigh vein) blood from the same body; a blood sample taken in life (one case); earlier samples from the same body
lines.outcome: Size and direction of differences in measured drug concentration between sampling sites and over time after death
lines.magnitude: Within one body (four selected overdoses, autopsy about 7 to 48 h after death): highest to lowest systemic-blood value 3.5- to 6.6-fold (excluding the separately reported portal values) per drug taken in the overdose (editors' calculation; doxepin 3.5, amobarbital 6.0, secobarbital 6.5, pentobarbital 6.2, clomipramine 5.4, flurazepam 6.6, imipramine 4.4; lidocaine given in hospital 1.6). One case with a sample from life: post-mortem imipramine 4.1–18.1 mg/L against 2.3 mg/L in hospital, 1.8- to 7.9-fold. Medians across drug-specific medians of paired within-case ratios (printed number of results): other blood 1.27 (576), muscle 0.99 (385), vitreous humour 0.45 (356), brain 1.84 (565), heart 2.03 (185), kidney 2.86 (401), lung 3.69 (187), spleen 4.25 (71), liver 5.06 (1,697), bile 5.52 (537); between drugs, liver 0.95–54.29, vitreous 0.03–1.59, other blood 0.90–14.61; other blood for morphine 1.26 (53), methamphetamine 1.50 (9). Human repeated sampling: first sample on average 17 h after death (range 1–292 h) where reported or estimated; rises in femoral blood for about 12 drugs, falls for 5 (no sizes). Narrative-review approximate heart-to-peripheral values without case counts or per-value sources (82 numeric-labelled entries among 98 distinct labels, including a nicotine/cotinine annotation; two ranges): morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5–2.3; more than 10% above the compilation's paired other-blood median for 17 of 24 drugs in both (editors' comparison). No within-drug intervals are given. The Table 3 N columns sum to 4,960 but include one oxazepam brain count without a printed ratio; the counts are results, not distinct deaths.
lines.reasoning: A descriptive claim starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, which reaches the floor: very low. Strict reading: that drug levels can differ between sampling sites and change after death is shown consistently by independent designs (a case series with a sample from life, a large compilation of paired values, repeated-sampling studies as reviewed) and on its own would be rated low; the sizes, and how often a change matters in an ordinary death, are very low. Status replicated: Pounder & Jones and the primary studies compiled by Ketola & Kriikku and reviewed by Borra et al. are independent and agree in direction. Counted once: Pounder & Jones is one of the compilation's doxepin sources; Ferner (2008) takes its heart-to-femoral ratios from Leikin & Watson (2003), so the narrative reviews' ratios are one source, used only as second-hand examples.

lines.q: Can drug levels change after death?
lines.short: Yes. Levels can rise or fall after death and differ between blood vessels, so a drug can look more or less involved in a death than it was.
lines.but: Nobody knows how often, or by how much, levels change in an ordinary death.
how: In four suspected overdose deaths picked as examples, a drug's level could be 3.5 to 6.6 times higher in one blood vessel than another in the same body. A hospital medicine varied only 1.6 times.
In one person, all imipramine samples after death were about 2 to 8 times the earlier hospital level.
A collection of 5,375 cases from published reports and Finnish lab records found that the gap between samples from different body parts varied more than tenfold between drugs.
In bodies tested more than once, levels of about a dozen drugs rose, including fentanyl and methadone; others, like THC, fell. First samples came about 17 hours after death on average.
lines.q_on_site_now: Can drug levels change after death?

lines.statement: In laboratory tests of urine fentanyl test strips used on dissolved drug and read by trained staff, compared with laboratory analysis (GC/MS) of the same samples or with the known content of prepared solutions, the strips showed fentanyl in almost every sample that contained it, down to very low concentrations, but the lowest concentration they detected differed widely between studies, brands, production lots and reading rules. In 106 police-seized samples that earlier GC/MS had found to contain fentanyl (two US forensic laboratories, 2017), one brand (BTNX Rapid Response) read positive in 104 (52 of 52 in one laboratory, 52 of 54 in the other; 98 in 100, editors' Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%); both samples it missed contained fentanyl alone. Because the forensic GC/MS methods were less sensitive than the strip (3.1 and 100 µg/mL), only samples with enough fentanyl for GC/MS to find could enter this positive group, so how often strips miss samples with very little fentanyl was not measured (Green et al., 2020). Second-hand figures, relayed without their conditions, mostly point the same way: in British Columbia drug-checking data, 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive samples were missed, all with fentanyl at 5% by weight or less (McCrae et al., 2020, as cited by Halifax et al., 2024); a scoping review relays sensitivity of about 96 to 98 in 100 from that study and one validation study (Kutscher et al., 2024); and another paper relays 87.5 in 100 from a validation study (Ti et al., 2020, as cited by Klaire et al., 2022). In pure fentanyl solutions, the lowest concentration detected was 100 to 150 ng/mL (Green et al., standards prepared in ethanol); 25 ng/mL by eye with five strips per concentration, counting a faint test band as positive (the pictured strips at 25 and 50 ng/mL show a faint band, which the makers' rule, any visible band means negative, reads as negative; Lockwood et al., 2021); positive at 100 ng/mL on all four brands in the main table, two of them with only a barely visible test band that the makers' rule reads as negative, and, in a descending series pictured for two brands, down to 50 and 25 ng/mL by the authors' rule (100 and 50 ng/mL by the makers' rule), with no replicates reported and one brand graded differently at 100 ng/mL in the table and the figure (Bergh et al., 2021); 20 ng/mL for two lots obtained in 2017 against 200 ng/mL for three lots obtained in 2021 (Halifax et al., 2024, duplicate strips); and 500 ng/mL for strips whose listed cut-off was 200 ng/mL, from a heat sub-study only (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024): a 25-fold range overall (editors' calculation). The seized samples were selected on known content and tested as powders by chemists blind to it, nearly all data come from one brand, and none of these studies measured how people prepare and read strips at home. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: Drug samples in laboratories: 210 police-seized samples from two US cities (2017), drug-checking samples in British Columbia (second-hand) and fentanyl reference standards dissolved in water or ethanol
lines.exposure: Urine fentanyl immunoassay test strips used off-label on dissolved drug (mostly BTNX Rapid Response; four brands in one study), read by trained laboratory staff
lines.comparator: Earlier forensic GC/MS analysis of the same samples, or the known concentration of prepared solutions
lines.outcome: Whether the strip showed fentanyl when it was present (sensitivity), and the lowest fentanyl concentration it detected
lines.magnitude: Seized samples (Green et al., 2020): sensitivity 100.0% (52/52) and 96.3% (52/54) at the two laboratories; 104/106 = 98.1% pooled (Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%, editors' calculation); reference GC/MS limits 3.1 and 100 µg/mL. Lowest concentration detected in pure fentanyl solutions: 0.100–0.150 mcg/mL, that is 100–150 ng/mL (Green et al., standards in ethanol); 25 ng/mL by eye, counting a faint band (Lockwood et al., 2021); positive at 100 ng/mL on four brands, two with a barely visible band only, and in a pictured series down to 50 ng/mL (Rapid Response) and 25 ng/mL (One Step) by the authors' rule, 100 and 50 ng/mL by the makers' rule (Bergh et al., 2021); 20 ng/mL for 2017 lots and 200 ng/mL for 2021 lots (Halifax et al., 2024); 500 ng/mL, listed cut-off 200 ng/mL, heat sub-study only (Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024). Second-hand: 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive drug-checking samples missed (McCrae et al., 2020, via Halifax et al.); sensitivity about 96.3–98% (via Kutscher et al., 2024); 87.5% (Ti et al., 2020, via Klaire et al., 2022).
lines.reasoning: Test-accuracy evidence that compares the strip with a reference method starts high (METHODS §6.3, test accuracy); one level each for risk of bias and indirectness gives low. Rated as worded: laboratory detection of fentanyl in seized samples with enough fentanyl for GC/MS and in pure solutions, not home use and not effects on behaviour or overdose, which are separate questions. Status replicated: independent teams in five laboratories (Green et al.; Lockwood et al.; Bergh et al.; Halifax et al.; Sisco, Appley, et al., 2024) detected fentanyl at ng/mL concentrations; only Green et al. measured sensitivity on seized samples. Overlap: the review's sensitivity range comes from a study sharing authors with Green et al. and from the drug-checking data cited by Halifax et al., so it is not counted separately, and the figure relayed by Klaire et al. is second-hand and not counted. Sisco, Appley, et al. (2024) is re-filed as test-accuracy with QUADAS-2 in this round (card sc_sisco_2024b) and adds one detection limit, from its heat sub-study.

lines.q: Do fentanyl test strips show fentanyl when it is there?
lines.short: Almost always, in lab tests: 98 in 100 seized drug samples with fentanyl showed it on the strip.
lines.but: Lab staff did these tests, mostly with one brand. Testing at home was not studied.
how: Two labs tested strips on 106 police-seized drug samples that had fentanyl. The strips showed it in 104.
A lab machine had already found fentanyl in all of these samples. Samples with very little fentanyl were not tested this way.
Strips can find very small amounts of fentanyl. But the smallest amount found differed up to 25 times between studies and batches.
It also depended on how a faint line was read. Trained staff did all of these tests.
lines.q_on_site_now: Do fentanyl test strips show fentanyl when it is there?

lines.statement: Other drugs are often detected in deaths labelled heroin overdose, but detection does not establish which substances caused a death. A 1996 narrative review, with no stated search or appraisal, selected medical-examiner and coroner series and statistics from the USA, Australia and Europe, mostly published 1967–1996, leaning on the authors’ 152 deaths in New South Wales in 1992. It relays morphine as the only drug detected in 23%–48% across six series and alcohol in 29%–75% across 13, with mean blood alcohol 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL where reported. Diazepam was detected in 12% in one cited study; this is a diazepam-specific result, not sole exposure; three others reported benzodiazepines in 22%, 27% and 55%. These are second-hand findings with unknown laboratory panels and varying death definitions, not shares proved to have been caused by heroin alone or by combinations (Darke & Zador, 1996). Five cited studies reported lower blood morphine when alcohol was detected. Correlations were weak where given: −0.14 in 505 alcohol-positive deaths and −0.28 in the authors’ series. A third of their series was below the laboratories’ 0.16 mg/L toxic level for people without opioid tolerance. A Michigan series published in 1977 reported 74% with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died from other causes; the review does not establish its case-collection dates. It cites three publications about survivor comparisons without numerical results or enough detail to establish independent samples and says better living-versus-fatal comparisons would add substantially to knowledge (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand). In the authors’ series 14% were classed as instant deaths and 22% took more than 3 hours; other series reported 44% beyond 2 hours and 52% beyond 3 hours. Other people were present in more than half of deaths in four studies (58%–79% where specified). The reviewers infer that combined drug toxicity explains many deaths. The editors’ limitation is that presence alone does not establish causal shares, tolerance was not measured, and delayed death is another possible explanation for low morphine. Darke and Zador do not discuss post-mortem redistribution; that separate limitation comes from toxicology literature, not their conclusions. The post-mortem result alone cannot decide the cause (Darke & Zador, 1996; Borra et al., 2026). In England and Wales in 2000, researchers reclassified1,037 accidental drug-related deaths voluntarily reported by coroners to a register of unstated completeness. They assigned 802 (77%) to direct overdose and 235 (23%) to other categories: 74 acute physical events, 112 toxicity with a medical condition, 31 traumatic accidents and 18 acute infections. Direct overdose was the default when no evidence suggested otherwise. These are recorded classifications. A ceiling for direct overdose and a floor for alternatives would be the editors’ conditional interpretation, assuming the other classifications were correct; neither is a validated bound on true causes or a measured error rate in official statistics (Webb et al., 2003). Heroin/morphine was recorded as implicated in 424 of 802 direct overdoses and detected in 488; it was implicated in 42 of 74 acute physical events, 33 of 72 deaths with a drug-related medical condition, and 11 of 18 infections. Alcohol was detected in 316 of 802 direct overdoses (39.4%), but the register recorded it only alongside other drugs. Methadone was implicated in 13% of direct overdoses, as the sole implicated drug in 4%; sole implication does not mean no other drug was detected. Negative findings were not recorded, leaving absence versus lack of testing uncertain (Webb et al., 2003). Heroin exposure can also be missed. A review reports falling femoral-blood 6-MAM, a heroin marker, between post-mortem samples in one primary study. It also relays both higher and lower post-mortem opioid concentrations compared with samples from life, with additional timing, specimen and morphine-transformation limits (Borra et al., 2026). Another review’s table says cerebrospinal-fluid 6-MAM detected 46% more heroin-related cases than blood, but supplies no case counts or unique per-value primary citation; this is a second-hand testing comparison, not 46% more proven heroin-caused deaths (Leikin & Watson, 2003). The main death-series figures are historical and cannot describe current drug mixtures or yield a rate per use. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: Deaths attributed to heroin overdose by medical examiners, coroners or researchers in series from the USA, Australia and Europe, mostly 1967–1996 (second-hand, Darke & Zador, 1996); 1,037 accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners in England and Wales to a national register in 2000 (Webb et al., 2003)
lines.exposure: Heroin use, shown by morphine (and where tested 6-MAM) found after death; other drugs found or named as implicated
lines.comparator: Morphine-only detection against co-detection; a Michigan series published 1977 comparing other-cause deaths (secondary); direct-overdose default category against alternative categories in England/Wales 2000
lines.outcome: What else was found in deaths attributed to heroin overdose, the timing and circumstances of death, and the mechanism of death
lines.magnitude: Secondary review: morphine-only 23%–48% across 6 series; alcohol 29%–75% across 13, mean 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL; diazepam detected in 12% in one cited series, benzodiazepines 22%, 27%, 55% in 3 others. Correlations −0.14 in 505 alcohol-positive deaths and −0.28. One series: a third below 0.16 mg/L, instant 14%, over 3 h 22%; other series over 2 h 44%, over 3 h 52%; others present 58%–79%. Michigan paper published 1977: 74% no higher than comparison deaths. England/Wales 2000: 1,037; default direct-overdose classification 802/1,037=77.3% and alternatives 235/1,037=22.7% (editors’ calculations); any ceiling/floor interpretation assumes the other assignments were correct and is not a validated bound on true causes or official-statistics errors. Heroin/morphine implicated 424/802, detected 488/802; implicated 42/74 acute events, 33/72 drug-related conditions, 11/18 infections. Alcohol co-detected 316/802=39.4%; methadone implicated 107/802≈13%, sole implicated 4% (sole implication, not sole detection). CSF comparison 46% more heroin-related cases, secondary and without counts; not deaths proved caused by heroin.
lines.reasoning: A descriptive claim starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS§6.3); unchanged risk-of-bias and indirectness downgrades give very low. Replicated describes repeated co-detection/alternative mechanisms across historical series and a separate register, not replication of a causal share. The same primary series relayed by a review is counted once. Sole detection, sole implication and causal attribution remain distinct. Draft retained.

lines.q: Are heroin overdose deaths always caused by heroin alone?
lines.short: Not necessarily. Older studies often found other drugs too: alcohol in 29 to 75 in 100 of these deaths. But finding a drug doesn't show it caused the death.
lines.but: These old records cannot tell how many deaths heroin alone caused.
how: In older studies from the USA, Australia and Europe, morphine was the only drug found in 23 to 48 in 100 deaths labelled heroin overdose. Alcohol was found in 29 to 75 in 100.
Many deaths took hours, and other people were often there: more than half the time, in four studies. These come second-hand, from a review.

In England and Wales in 2000, researchers classed 23 in 100 accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners as something other than a direct overdose, like an infection, an injury, or drug effects plus an illness.
Heroin use can also be missed, because its marker can fall after death. Levels also depend on where and when blood is taken.
lines.q_on_site_now: Are heroin overdose deaths always caused by heroin alone?

lines.statement: The US Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee, meeting on 4 June 2024 on Lykos Therapeutics' new drug application for MDMA (midomafetamine) capsules with a psychological intervention for PTSD, voted 9 to 2 that the available data did not show the drug to be effective and 10 to 1 that its benefits, with the FDA's proposed risk-mitigation programme, did not outweigh its risks (the FDA's final summary minutes, approved on 26 July 2024).
