Members cited functional unblinding, unmanaged expectation bias and selection bias; a follow-up too confounded to show durability; the lack of a factorial design separating the drug from the psychotherapy, and the therapists' unblinding and power of suggestion; and, on safety, missing laboratory, QTc and cardiac data, inadequate data on abuse liability and diversion, hyponatremia and the risk of boundary violations; the two members voting yes weighed the large effect sizes. The FDA reviewers' own briefing document, pre-decisional, had put the same issues to the committee: in MAPP2 94% of the MDMA arm and 75% of the placebo arm guessed their allocation and the in-session monitors could probably tell it too; the only outcome after 18 weeks came from an observational visit the FDA judged not designed to evaluate durability; no study separated the effect of the psychotherapy; the QT assessment was incomplete and phase 3 had no laboratory tests on dosing days; and the sponsor had not recorded positive drug effects such as euphoria as adverse events, against the FDA's advice of 2017, which the reviewers said limited the assessment of abuse potential. The decision itself is known only second-hand: as described in a BMJ news report and two later papers, the FDA declined in August 2024 to approve the application and, according to the company, asked for another phase 3 trial (the month is given by a 2025 commentary citing CNN; the decision letter was not read); the BMJ, published on 13 August 2024, says the decision came before the three phase 2 retractions by Psychopharmacology (see the retraction claim in this section). A 2025 paper, citing news reports and an article in JAMA, calls the vote split, and its unsourced statement that the rejection cited weaknesses in safety documentation and in adverse-event reporting is consistent with the reviewers' briefing but not shown by it. The BMJ also states, without a source, that the research in the three retracted papers did not form part of the application; the FDA's briefing bases efficacy on the phase 3 trials and lists phase 2 studies among the sources of its safety data, without naming the retracted analyses or the study site (MP4) behind the retractions; the sponsor's own briefing document for the committee likewise cites none of the three analyses and lists the phase 2 study MP-4 among the 17 studies supporting the drug's safety but not among the six it pooled for its safety analyses (Lykos Therapeutics, 2024). The same document dates the FDA's agreement on the phase 3 design (a Special Protocol Assessment, July 2017) and Breakthrough Therapy Designation (August 2017), the final part of the rolling application to December 2023 and the FDA's filing of it, with Priority Review, to February 2024. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: The US regulatory review of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD (2024)
lines.exposure: Lykos Therapeutics' new drug application for MDMA capsules for PTSD
lines.outcome: The advisory committee's votes and stated reasons and the FDA reviewers' concerns (from the FDA's own documents); the FDA decision as reported second-hand
lines.magnitude: Not a quantity. Advisory committee votes (final summary minutes; 11 voting members): effectiveness, yes 2, no 9, abstain 0; benefit-risk with the FDA's proposed REMS, yes 1, no 10, abstain 0. Decision: declined in August 2024 (second-hand; the month from a 2025 commentary citing a CNN report).
lines.reasoning: A descriptive claim about documented events, rated as a description (METHODS §6.3): it starts low. Risk of bias, one level: the committee's votes and reasons and the FDA reviewers' concerns now rest on the FDA's own final summary minutes and briefing document, read in full; but the decision itself, its month, its reasons and what the FDA asked for are known only from a news report, the company's statements as relayed, a commentary citing a CNN report and a qualitative study's background statements citing news reports and an article in JAMA, because the decision letter was not read, and two statements (that the rejection cited weaknesses in safety documentation and adverse-event reporting; that the retracted research was not part of the application) have no source; the claim inherits this weakest necessary link (METHODS §6.3). Inconsistency not rated down: the sources agree on the decision; the minutes' counts (9 to 2 and 10 to 1) match the BMJ's summary, and the 2025 study's split vote is a loose description of them. Indirectness not rated down because the statement says which parts are second-hand. Status single study: the account of the meeting rests on one set of FDA documents, that of the decision on one news report, and the other sources cite news reports. The three retractions, documented by the journal's own notices, are a separate claim since the adjudication of 2026-10-17.

lines.q: Did the US regulator approve MDMA therapy for PTSD in 2024?
lines.short: No. The US regulator turned it down in August 2024, after its expert panel voted 9 to 2 that the data didn't show it works.
lines.but: We read the panel's notes, but not the final letter.
how: In June 2024, the regulator's expert panel voted 9 to 2 that the data didn't show the treatment works, and 10 to 1 that the benefits didn't outweigh the risks.
Panel members worried that people could tell which pill they'd had. In one trial, 94 in 100 on MDMA and 75 in 100 on the dummy pill guessed right.
They also doubted the later check of whether benefits lasted, and noted that no study separated the drug's effect from the therapy's.
The regulator's own staff said the main trials had no lab tests on treatment days, and the company didn't log euphoria as a side effect, so misuse risk was harder to judge.
lines.q_on_site_now: Did the US regulator approve MDMA therapy for PTSD in 2024?

lines.statement: In school students in grades 5 to 12 (no country given; the review presents D.A.R.E. as a US programme), in 11 controlled evaluations published in journals between 1991 and 2002 (236 to 2,878 students each, 11,505 listed in all, editors' sum; experimental and quasi-experimental designs, the review not saying which were which), the original Project D.A.R.E. (Drug Abuse Resistance Education) school curriculum compared with each study's control or comparison condition does not detectably change self-reported use of alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs, combined into one effect per study, measured from immediately after the programme to 10 years later: pooled d = 0.023 (95% CI −0.04 to 0.08; r = 0.011; z = 0.73, not significant), below the level usually considered small (West & O'Neal, 2004; no funding statement). In 8 of the 11 studies the interval included no difference (editors' count from Table 1); the largest, of 2,878 fifth graders, found slightly more use in the D.A.R.E. group (d = −0.117, −0.19 to −0.04), and two small studies found less (395 sixth graders, d = 0.376, 0.07 to 0.68; 236 fifth and sixth graders, smoking the only outcome, d = 0.405, 0.01 to 0.80). Four of the 11 effects, covering 4,539 of the 11,505 students listed (39%, editors' sum) and including the only 10-year follow-up, were not computed but entered as zero and footnoted as assumed. The review did not appraise its studies, names no pooling model and reports no heterogeneity; a random-effects pooling of its printed values reproduces its estimate, while a fixed-effect pooling gives d = −0.005 (−0.043 to 0.034), so the near-zero result does not depend on the model (editors' recalculation; study estimates vary more than chance would predict, I² about 54%). Many included studies analysed individual students although students were nested in schools, which the authors say tends to overestimate effectiveness and judge unlikely to change the result; ignoring the clustering also makes the pooled interval narrower than it should be (editors' note). Every study evaluated the original curriculum: D.A.R.E. was substantially revamped in 2001, and the authors found no evaluation of the new version, so this answer does not apply to it. The authors' remark that the effect would have needed to be 20 times larger to count as small overstates the gap: Cohen's small benchmarks are about 9 times the pooled values (editors' calculation). An earlier meta-analysis, as the paper describes it, found negligible effects (0.00 to 0.11) immediately after the programme. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: School students in grades 5 to 12 (no country given in the review, which presents D.A.R.E. as a US programme; 236 to 2,878 per study; 11,505 listed across the 11 studies, editors' sum) in 11 controlled evaluations (experimental or quasi-experimental, not distinguished in the review) published in peer-reviewed journals from 1991 to 2002
lines.exposure: The original Project D.A.R.E. school curriculum, before its 2001 revision; content, number of sessions and delivery not described in the review
lines.comparator: Each study's control or comparison condition, not described in the review
lines.outcome: Self-reported use of alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs, combined into one effect per study, from immediately after the programme to 10 years later
lines.magnitude: West & O'Neal (2004): pooled r = 0.011, d = 0.023 (95% CI −0.04 to 0.08; the interval is on the d scale, editors' check), z = 0.73, not significant; positive values favour D.A.R.E. Study effects (Table 1): Becker 1992 d = −0.117 (−0.19 to −0.04; 2,878 students); Zagumny & Thompson 1997 d = 0.376 (0.07 to 0.68; 395); Ahmed 2002 d = 0.405 (0.01 to 0.80; 236; smoking only); four effects entered as assumed zeros (Ennett 1994, Rosenbaum 1994, Wysong 1994, Lynam 1999; 4,539 of 11,505 students, 39%, editors' sum); 8 of 11 intervals include zero (editors' count). Editors' recalculation from the printed d values and intervals: random-effects (DerSimonian–Laird) d = 0.023 (−0.039 to 0.085), reproducing the published estimate; fixed-effect d = −0.005 (−0.043 to 0.034); Q = 21.6 on 10 df (P about 0.02), I² about 54%. Cohen's small benchmarks (d = 0.2, r = 0.1) are about 8.7 and 9.1 times the pooled values (editors' calculation), against the paper's 20 times. No absolute difference in the share of students using any substance can be given.
lines.reasoning: The review admitted experimental and quasi-experimental designs without saying which studies were randomized, so the evidence cannot be treated as randomized and starts low; seen only through this review, which did not appraise its studies, it is rated down one level for risk of bias (METHODS §6.3), giving very low, the floor. Rated as worded: no detectable effect of the original curriculum on self-reported use of alcohol, tobacco and illegal drugs combined; the pooled effect is near zero (d = 0.023) with an interval that excludes Cohen's small benchmark, and a fixed-effect pooling gives −0.005 (editors' recalculation). The very low rating reflects how little this single brief review lets anyone check (designs not reported, four effects assumed, clustering ignored), not a sign of a hidden benefit: the biases expected in such studies would favour D.A.R.E. The authors' remark that the effect would need to be 20 times larger to count as small is not adopted (about 9 times, editors' calculation). Status replicated: the review reports each study's direction, and in 8 of 11 independent evaluations the interval included no difference; the earlier meta-analysis, described in the paper but not read, agrees and is not counted. The answer does not cover the curriculum revised in 2001.

lines.q: Did the original DARE school programme stop young people using drugs?
lines.short: No. Across 11 studies of the original DARE school classes, kids who had DARE used alcohol, tobacco and other drugs about as much as kids who didn't.
lines.but: Only the original classes were tested: DARE was rebuilt in 2001, and that version wasn't part of this review.
how: A 2004 review combined 11 studies, published 1991 to 2002, of 11,505 students in grades 5 to 12, comparing those who had DARE with those who didn't.
Students who had DARE used alcohol, tobacco and other drugs about as much as others, from right after the classes to 10 years later.
In 8 of the 11 studies, the result couldn't be told apart from no difference. Two small ones found less use with DARE; the biggest, of 2,878 students, found slightly more.
Four results, including the only 10-year one, weren't worked out but filled in as zero.
lines.q_on_site_now: Did the original DARE school programme stop young people using drugs?

lines.statement: In US household surveys from 2002 to 2016 (National Surveys on Drug Use and Health), among people who had first used cocaine less than 12 months before the interview, an estimated 5.0% (95% CI 4.0% to 6.3%) of those who had used only powder, and 22.2% (16.7% to 29.4%) of those who had gone on to crack, met DSM-IV criteria for cocaine dependence by the time they were interviewed; the estimates are summaries of seven two-year survey pairs (2014 is not among them), based on the paper's unweighted totals of 3,488 powder-only and 275 powder-then-crack initiates, which its Methods describe as effective sample sizes back-calculated from the survey output (9 to 96 per year-pair in the second group). Of 21 dependence-related problems asked about, the most frequent in both groups was wanting or trying to cut down or stop using cocaine (45.4%, 43.1% to 47.9%, against 58.3%, 53.0% to 64.2%) and the least frequent was continuing to use despite physical problems caused or worsened by cocaine (1.9% against 2.8%, the difference not significant); most of the other problems were more common in the group who had gone on to crack, with at least one exception and one item whose estimate the paper does not plot. The two groups are not comparable exposures: the comparison is unadjusted, the survey asks about cocaine in any form rather than which form caused a problem, and reaching crack within the same 12 months takes time and continued use, so time since first use, which is not reported for either group, and amount used may differ. The paper's authors give three readings of the difference without choosing between them: people who go on to crack may be more susceptible from the outset; some may become dependent on powder and then start crack; or something about crack smoking may raise the risk. Dependence was scored against DSM-IV criteria from people's own answers in a computer interview, in a household and group-quarters survey (people in institutions are outside the sampling frame), without characteristics reported for either group, and the item wording sits in supplements that were not available. The 22% is not shown to be the same as the roughly 30% reported for newly started heroin use in a separate study: no test is reported and the interval stops at 29.4%. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People aged 12 and over in US households and non-institutional group quarters who had first used cocaine less than 12 months before interview, 2002–2016 National Surveys on Drug Use and Health (seven two-year pairs; 2014 not included): 3,488 powder-only and 275 powder-then-crack initiates in all (effective sample sizes per two-year pair 194–590 and 9–96)
lines.exposure: Having first used cocaine within the past 12 months: powder only, or powder followed by crack (self-reported)
lines.comparator: People who had started powder cocaine and never used crack (unadjusted comparison)
lines.outcome: Meeting DSM-IV criteria for cocaine dependence, and 21 dependence-related problems, by the time of interview
lines.magnitude: Chandra & Anthony (2020), meta-analysis summaries of seven two-year survey pairs: dependence within 1–12 months of first use 5.0% (95% CI 4.0% to 6.3%) in powder-only initiates and 22.2% (16.7% to 29.4%) in powder-then-crack initiates (the paper's Conclusions print 20% for the second). Year-pair estimates 2.9% to 7.0% and 10.3% to 30.0%, the widest interval running from 9.2% to 64.5%. Problem items: wanting or trying to cut down or stop 45.4% (43.1% to 47.9%) against 58.3% (53.0% to 64.2%), difference p < 0.05; continuing to use despite physical problems 1.9% (1.6% to 2.4%) against 2.8% (1.6% to 5.2%), p > 0.05. The study card's reading of the figure: powder-only estimates below 10% for 17 of the 20 plotted items, powder-then-crack estimates 15% or more for 14; one item about equal in the two groups and one (about 36% against 28%) higher in the powder-only group. No adjusted estimate, no absolute difference with an interval and no per-month risk are given.
lines.reasoning: A descriptive claim (relation 'describes') about how many people meet dependence criteria starts low (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1 and imprecision −1 take it below the floor: very low. Status single study: one analysis of one survey series. The direction of the powder-crack difference agrees with an earlier analysis by the same research group of 1995–1998 survey data (Chen & Anthony, 2004, used in the answer on crack and powder), which is not independent, and a 2017 systematic review, which includes the 2004 analysis but predates this one, describes crack-versus-other-cocaine comparisons on dependence as mixed (Butler et al., 2017). Not used, following the study card: any statement that smoking crack causes the excess, any per-month risk, and the comparison with heroin.

lines.q: How fast can you get hooked on cocaine?
lines.short: Within a year of starting, about 5 in 100 who used only powder were dependent; 22 in 100 who went on to crack.
lines.but: People answered once, about themselves. The survey cannot show that crack itself made the difference.
how: US surveys from 2002 to 2016 asked people who had first used cocaine less than a year before.
About 5 in 100 of those who had used only powder met the criteria for cocaine dependence. So did about 22 in 100 of those who had gone on to crack.
In both groups the most common problem was wanting or trying to cut down or stop: about 45 in 100 and 58 in 100.
People who go on to crack may differ to begin with, and some may already have had problems with powder. The survey did not ask which form caused a problem.
lines.q_on_site_now: How quickly can dependence start after first using cocaine?

lines.statement: In 166 healthy, screened adults aged 18 to 45 who took MDMA in a hospital research unit in Basel (nine double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies from one laboratory), a single dose raised blood pressure, heart rate and ear temperature above placebo in the same people over the next 6 hours. At 125 mg (136 people) the average highest systolic pressure was 157 mm Hg against 133 on placebo, the average highest heart rate 95 beats a minute against 76, and the average highest ear temperature 37.7 degrees Celsius against 37.4. Systolic pressure went above 160 mm Hg in 38 in 100 people against 6 in 100 on placebo, and above 180 in 5 in 100 against none; heart rate went above 100 in 33 in 100 against 2; ear temperature went above 38 degrees in 24 in 100 against 9 (editors' calculation: with MDMA, 32, 31 and 15 more in 100 people crossed the lines for systolic pressure above 160, heart rate above 100 and temperature above 38). The highest values were 196 mm Hg systolic, 145 beats a minute and 39.1 degrees; the paper reports no temperature above 40 degrees, no hypertensive urgency and no other sign of a hypertensive crisis (severe headache, shortness of breath, nosebleed). At 75 mg (30 people) the rises were smaller (systolic 145 against 131 mm Hg; temperature 37.2 against 37.0, not marked as significant); that comparison is between different people in different studies, and the difference between doses was significant for blood pressure but not for heart rate or temperature. Peaks came on average 1.7 to 2.4 hours after the dose. Laboratory studies from several groups, as summarized in a narrative review (second-hand), report a temperature rise that grows with dose (+0.1, +0.4 and +0.7 degrees on average at doses up to 1.0, 1.1 to 1.9 and 2.0 mg/kg), and one of 13 volunteers in an earlier study had a brief hypertensive crisis (240/145 mm Hg for 20 minutes). These sessions differ from real life: people rested, with a research assistant present, in a room at about 22.7 degrees Celsius; they took MDMA of known amount and no other drug, were healthy, four in five were new to MDMA, and no one took a second dose in the same session. Heat, dancing, crowding, other drugs, pills of unknown content and extra doses were not tested, and the study was too small to rule out events as frequent as 1 in 100 (for no temperature above 40 degrees in 278 sessions, the 95% interval runs from 0 to 1.3 in 100). Four people reported no effect of the drug and were left out of the analysis of when the felt effects began and ended; the paper does not say what their blood pressure, heart rate or temperature did. Everyone was given a fixed dose, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested here (controlled studies of a second dose are covered in separate claims); the authors, citing earlier studies, argue that effects fade while MDMA is still in the body (acute tolerance) and that adding more may not lengthen the effect but may add adverse effects, which is their reading and not a result of this analysis.
lines.population: 166 healthy adults aged 18 to 45 (equal numbers of women and men; mean age 24.5; four in five new to MDMA), psychiatrically screened, mostly recruited on a university campus and paid, in nine studies at one hospital in Basel: 30 people in the 75 mg study and 136 in the 125 mg studies
lines.exposure: A single oral dose of MDMA hydrochloride in capsules, taken at rest in a research unit with a research assistant present, room temperature 22.7 (SD 0.6) degrees Celsius (study conditions: 75 mg in 30 people; 125 mg in 136 people, 112 of whom took 125 mg a second time at least seven days later after a pretreatment medicine, a session not analysed here)
lines.comparator: Placebo in the same people on another day (double-blind crossover); for the 75 against 125 mg contrast, different people in different studies
lines.outcome: Highest blood pressure, heart rate and ear (tympanic) temperature in the 6 hours after the dose, and the number of people whose highest value crossed a clinical line (systolic above 160 or 180 mm Hg, heart rate above 100 beats a minute, temperature above 38 or 40 degrees Celsius)
lines.magnitude: 125 mg (n = 136), average of each person's highest value in 6 hours, MDMA against placebo (SD): systolic 157 (15) against 133 (15) mm Hg; diastolic 93 (10) against 79 (8); heart rate 95 (17) against 76 (12) beats a minute; ear temperature 37.7 (0.5) against 37.4 (0.5) degrees Celsius; drug effect p < 0.001 for each. People above the line, MDMA against placebo: systolic >160 mm Hg 51 (38%) against 8 (6%); >180 7 (5%) against 0; heart rate >100 45 (33%) against 3 (2%); temperature >38 32 (24%) against 12 (9%). Highest single values: 196 against 175 mm Hg, 145 against 117 beats a minute, 39.1 against 38.7 degrees. 75 mg (n = 30): systolic 145 (14) against 131 (11); diastolic 84 (8) against 77 (5); heart rate 83 (17) against 69 (9); temperature 37.2 (0.3) against 37.0 (0.3), no significance mark; >160 mm Hg 3 (10%) against 0; heart rate >100 3 (10%) against 0; temperature >38 none. Dose-by-drug tests: systolic F 15.2 and diastolic F 17.9 (p < 0.001); heart rate F 2.38 and temperature F 2.43 (not significant). All 166 sessions: systolic >160 in 54 (33%), >180 in 7 (4%); heart rate >100 in 48 (29%); temperature >38 in 32 (19%); no temperature above 40 and no hypertensive urgency. Editors' calculation: at 125 mg, 32, 31 and 15 more in 100 people crossed the lines for systolic pressure above 160 mm Hg, heart rate above 100 and temperature above 38 degrees with MDMA than on placebo. Laboratory studies summarized in a narrative review: peak rise in core temperature +0.1 (doses up to 1.0 mg/kg), +0.4 (1.1 to 1.9 mg/kg), +0.7 (2.0 mg/kg).
lines.reasoning: Placebo-controlled double-blind within-person laboratory studies start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias 0. Moderate for the statement that a single dose of 125 mg raised blood pressure, heart rate and ear temperature above placebo in healthy volunteers at rest. The shares above each line are descriptive: they count people whose highest of many readings crossed a line, and 9 in 100 placebo sessions also crossed 38 degrees, so the lines show how many people went over them and not a threshold of harm. The 75 against 125 mg contrast rests on different people in different studies and is not tested for heart rate and temperature; the paper's abstract and Conclusion call all three shares significantly greater at 125 mg, and this claim follows the tests instead. Status replicated by the same team: nine studies, one laboratory and one analysis model; other groups are seen only second-hand through a narrative review. The claim gives no advice, does not say whether the changes are harmful, and does not generalise to settings that were not tested.

lines.q: What does MDMA do to body temperature, heart and blood pressure?
lines.short: One dose pushes all three up. In lab tests, 24 in 100 people went over 38 degrees after MDMA, against 9 in 100 after a dummy pill.
lines.but: Healthy volunteers rested in a room at about 23 degrees. Heat, dancing, crowds, other drugs and extra doses weren't tested.
how: 136 healthy adults got one lab dose. The top blood-pressure number went above 160 in 38 in 100 after MDMA, against 6 in 100 after a dummy pill.
A heart rate above 100 happened in 33 in 100 after MDMA, against 2 in 100 after the dummy pill.
Ear temperature went above 38 degrees in 24 in 100 after MDMA, against 9 in 100; the highest was 39.1 degrees.
Four people felt no effect and the study does not say what their bodies did. Everyone got a set dose, so taking more was not tested here.

lines.statement: What makes body temperature rise more after MDMA is not settled. This claim rests on one narrative review (Parrott, 2012) of small studies, so its figures are second-hand and given as summarized by the review. In placebo-controlled laboratory studies of 4 to 16 volunteers each, the review puts the average peak rise in core temperature at +0.1 degrees Celsius at doses up to 1.0 mg/kg, +0.4 at 1.1 to 1.9 mg/kg and +0.7 at 2.0 mg/kg, from studies using different body sites; in the one study of 8 men that gave 75 mg and 125 mg, the peak was +0.4 at both. In two small studies at 2.0 mg/kg in rooms at 18 and 30 degrees, the rise was +1.0 and +0.8 in 4 volunteers and +0.4 and +0.6 in 10, which the review describes as nearly identical or broadly similar in the two rooms, although its own table of factors lists a high room temperature as associated with a higher core temperature. The rise differs between people: in 8 volunteers the group average was +0.4 but one person peaked at +1.9; at a dance party the two people with the highest MDMA blood levels (0.77 and 0.84 mg/l) had the largest rises (+1.0 and +1.6), while across 27 people the link between blood level and rise was borderline (r = +0.38, p = 0.058) and there was no night without MDMA to compare. In studies at dance clubs and parties, of 11 to 41 people each and with different comparisons, group peak rises ranged from +0.2 to +1.6 degrees (+1.8 on the skin in one), the largest in 11 people who took 6 tablets on average over a night; the review reports no comparison within them of amounts, dancing, room heat or crowding. It says data on dancing and on other drugs are very limited, that crowding and loud music have not been investigated, and that hydration, age, sex, genes and personality need to be investigated in people. Overheating to 40 degrees and above, some of it fatal, is known from hospital case reports, which cannot show how often it happens; in a UK report of 7 deaths and 4 further cases of this kind, plasma MDMA ranged from 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l, which its authors said did not reflect high doses, and in another case a friend who took the same MDMA had no thermal reaction. How hot people feel also differs: in an Internet survey of over 200 people who take ecstasy, 16 in 100 did not feel hot, 41 slightly, 31 moderately and 12 strongly or extremely, and the review offers as a hypothesis for future study that people with low thermal awareness might be most at risk. Some people feel little from an amount and take more; the review notes continuous dancing and bingeing for over 48 hours without sleep in experienced people with greater tolerance, and calls the effects of that currently unknown. In 166 volunteers resting at about 22.7 degrees (a pooled laboratory analysis), 125 mg raised the average highest ear temperature by 0.3 degrees (37.7 against 37.4) and 24 in 100 crossed 38 degrees against 9 in 100 on placebo; the test of a dose effect between 75 and 125 mg was not significant. Those volunteers rested, took one pure dose and were not dancing, crowded or on other drugs, so the laboratory studies cannot show what heat, dancing, crowding, other drugs or more MDMA do to temperature, and the party studies cannot separate them either.
lines.population: People given MDMA in placebo-controlled laboratory studies (4 to 16 volunteers each), people studied at dance clubs and house parties (11 to 41 each), and people treated in hospital for severe overheating (case reports and series), all as summarized in one narrative review; the 166 volunteers of one pooled laboratory analysis read in full as a qualifier
lines.exposure: MDMA, by dose in the laboratory (study conditions: up to 1.0, 1.1 to 1.9 and 2.0 mg/kg; 75 and 125 mg) and by tablets taken over a night in party studies (1 to 6 tablets, other drugs sometimes taken); room temperature (18 and 30 degrees Celsius in two studies), dancing, crowding, other drugs and hydration as possible modifiers
lines.comparator: Placebo in laboratory studies; an abstinent weekend, people not taking ecstasy at the same club, the evening before, or no comparison in the party studies
lines.outcome: Peak rise in core temperature (rectal, swallowed sensor, ear, mouth or armpit), in degrees Celsius; severe overheating (40 degrees Celsius and above)
lines.magnitude: Laboratory, peak change in core temperature, average across the studies in the review's table: +0.1 degrees Celsius (doses up to 1.0 mg/kg), +0.4 (1.1 to 1.9 mg/kg), +0.7 (2.0 mg/kg); different body sites, 4 to 16 volunteers per study, no intervals. In one study, 75 mg and 125 mg both +0.4 (8 men). Rooms at 18 and 30 degrees: +1.0 and +0.8 (4 volunteers) and +0.4 and +0.6 (10 volunteers). One study of 8 volunteers: group mean +0.4, highest individual +1.9. Dance clubs and parties, group peak change: +0.2 (27 people), +1.2 (32), +0.3 (12), +1.6 (11, 6 tablets on average), +1.1 oral and +1.8 skin (41); comparisons differ. One party study: blood level against rise r = +0.38, p = 0.058 (27 people). Internet survey of over 200 people: did not feel hot 16%, slightly 41%, moderately 31%, strongly or extremely 12%. Severe overheating (40 to 43 degrees): case reports and series only, no denominator. Laboratory study read in full, 125 mg against placebo (136 people): average highest ear temperature 37.7 against 37.4, above 38 degrees in 24% against 9%.
lines.reasoning: A claim seen only through a narrative review starts from the design of the primary studies the review describes (small placebo-controlled laboratory studies, uncontrolled party studies, case reports) and is downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness (METHODS 6.3). Observational start (low); down four levels in all (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision), bounded at very low. Relation: evidence is insufficient to say whether dose, heat, dancing, crowding, other drugs or hydration change the rise, because no study separates them and the review says so itself. Status mixed: party studies disagree in size without an explanation, and the review's table and text disagree about room temperature. Draft: the claim rests only on a narrative review (METHODS 6.3); the pooled laboratory analysis read in full is a qualifying anchor, and the single quotation is the review's hypothesis, which it marks as untested.

lines.q: Why do some people overheat on MDMA?
lines.short: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others with MDMA.
lines.but: This is second-hand, from one review of small studies. They couldn't tell heat, dancing and crowds apart.
how: In small lab studies of people at rest, body temperature rose about 0.4 degrees on average at medium doses and 0.7 at higher ones; one person in a group of 8 went up 1.9.
At clubs and parties the average rise ran from 0.2 to 1.6 degrees. But the review reports no comparison of amounts, dancing, room heat or crowds, so which matters is unknown.

Severe overheating (40 degrees and up, sometimes fatal) is known from hospital cases. In one UK report, blood levels didn't suggest high doses. In another case, a friend who took the same MDMA didn't overheat.
People also feel it differently: in one survey, 16 in 100 people who take ecstasy did not feel hot.
